title: How Do People Know If a Leader Is Sincere
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that sincerity, not authenticity, is the quality that actually earns trust for leaders in specific conversations. It breaks sincerity down into four simultaneous behaviors: maintaining direct eye contact, varying vocal tone and pace to signal conviction, choosing precise language that matches the belief being expressed, and aligning facial expressions and gestures with the message. The author notes these behaviors typically occur automatically when someone genuinely believes what they're saying, but leaders can become more intentional about deploying them when the stakes of a conversation are high. A closing quote from Emerson frames sincerity as a form of respect leaders owe to the people they lead. The piece ends by inviting readers to consider whether their own teams feel that sincerity when they speak.
points: Sincerity, more than authenticity, is what earns lasting trust from a leader's team
Four simultaneous signals project sincerity: eye contact, vocal variation, word choice, and matching nonverbal cues
Video review often reveals leaders maintain less eye contact, especially while listening, than they assume
Sincerity can be practiced and made more intentional, not just left to instinct
quotes: Authenticity gets all the press, but for leaders, sincerity matters more.
Sincere leaders operate with great consistency in their words and actions.
Direct eye contact is a sign of respect in most cultures and fosters trust and openness.
Second, they vary their pitch, tone, and inflection to emphasize their conviction.
Sincere leaders choose their words carefully to fully capture how they feel and what they believe.
A serious message requires serious expressions and gestures for it to be viewed as sincere, and so forth.
As the philosopher Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “Sincerity is the highest compliment you can pay.
